source.title: Harmony in Diversity: Merging Neural Networks with Canonical Correlation Analysis
source.authors: Stefan Horoi; Albert Manuel Orozco Camacho; Eugene Belilovsky; Guy Wolf

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures relationships between activations of independently initialized networks and evaluates linear CCA-based alignment, but it does not use the claim's scale-dependent distance-similarity test.
record.gate_note: Results bear on shared representations across independently initialized networks and on whether a linear alignment can support model merging. The authors also compare merging algorithms; the rows below record CCA Merge outcomes and direct activation-correlation results, not cited findings or baseline results alone.
record.test_reason: Mainly a model-merging methods paper, but Section 4.2 (Fig. 2) and Appendices B and E measure neuron-activation correlations between independently initialized same-architecture networks. This bears on V3: features are shared but not matched one-to-one at the unit level. The method resembles Li et al.'s correlation analysis, but the setting differs (ResNet20×8, CIFAR100). The merged-accuracy results measure parameter-averaging compatibility (linear mode connectivity), not representational mapping loss, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors add that neurons do not have exact one-to-one matches across networks. They argue that linear combinations (CCA) capture distributed features, giving better pairwise and multi-model merges. They note that the method needs shared input data and that merging models trained on entirely different datasets is future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses CCA-based activation alignment and evaluates parameter merging; it does not test scale-dependent convergence using distances between the same data points.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with model width, dataset and training-data split, number of models merged, and use of REPAIR. CCA regularization γ is selected using extra models for each architecture and dataset/data split.

fits_no_version.finding: After CCA alignment, averaging two independently initialized nets keeps most accuracy. Examples: VGG11 82.7–85.5% vs base 87–88%; ResNet20 31.8%→75.1% as width rises ×1→×8; ImageNet ResNet18×4 63.6% vs 75.4%. On disjoint data splits 1 and 2, merges slightly exceed the base-model average. Accuracy drops less than 4% when merging up to 20 models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently trained same-architecture networks can be linearly aligned so that parameter averaging retains much of their accuracy, with the barrier shrinking as width grows (linear mode connectivity beyond permutations).

record.problems: The direct correlation analysis is reported for ResNet20×8 on CIFAR100 and only two merging layers; the figure's underlying correlation values are not stated. Many multi-model scaling results are presented as plots, with only qualitative endpoint summaries in the text. The evaluated outcome is classification accuracy after parameter averaging, not a direct measure of general representational similarity. CCA requires shared input data, and the authors do not test entirely different training datasets.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out for the selected results. The paper reports many comparator-method accuracies; these were not included because the record focuses on CCA alignment outcomes and direct representation-correlation results. Figure 2/3 plotted point values and the per-count values in Figure 4 are unavailable in the text and are recorded only as figure-only or described aggregates.

untested.parts: All of it. Width varies only within a single architecture, and no cross-architecture, cross-objective or cross-data alignment is compared against capability.
All of it; no vision-language pairs are compared.
Subspace-level similarity scores (e.g. CCA coefficients as similarity) are not reported. The correlation analysis covers only ResNet20×8 on CIFAR100.
No direct measure of mapping loss (stitching, linear-probe transfer, relative representations). Merged accuracy conflates mapping with parameter averaging.
All of it; no interpretable features or circuits are examined.
All of it; no comparison of similarity metrics or out-of-distribution inputs.
All of it; the study gives no subspace-level completeness measure and no causal analysis of shared data or objectives.

missing.what: Permutation matching fails to pair 25–50% of neurons with their highest-correlated counterpart, evidence against one-to-one unit correspondence.
Unit matches are inconsistent across models: 50–80% of neurons are matched differently when aligned directly vs. through a third model (Permute).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 and V7 labels are dropped. Merged-model accuracy measures averaging compatibility, not representational interchangeability or the completeness of convergence. The width effect (wider models merge better) is within one architecture and is cited as already known (App. G), so it is not evidence for V1. r5's CCA value (85.54%) was misread as missing because the flattened table omits ZipIt! out-of-memory cells.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies network width, but does not measure whether representation alignment rises with model size or capability across different architectures, objectives, data, or modalities.
No paired image-caption vision-language representations are compared.
Tests independently initialized models of the same architecture, mainly ResNet20×8 on CIFAR100; it does not establish the claim across architectures, tasks, or broader feature types.
Tests CCA-derived linear transformations followed by parameter averaging and task-accuracy evaluation. It does not test stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired inputs.
The study analyzes activation correlations among neurons, but does not identify recurring interpretable features or circuits.
It varies datasets and training-data splits, but does not compare alternative representation-similarity metrics, metric settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
Results bear on whether alignment and merged-model performance are complete; the study does not establish that shared data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, explain alignment.

rows.subject: ResNet20×8 models A and B (two independently initialized models)
rows.operation_detail: Measured correlations between neurons' activations on a set of inputs.

conditions.value: two layers; exact layer names not stated

rows.measure: Distribution of pairwise neuron activation correlations; the text says top correlations are relatively high but none approaches 1.
rows.value: figure only; described as top correlations being relatively high but none approaching full correlation
rows.note: The authors interpret this as evidence that a feature in one model can be distributed across multiple neurons in the other, rather than having one exact highly correlated match.
rows.check: Remove V7. Top correlations are high but below 1, with features distributed across neurons. V3 expects exactly this (shared features, not the same units). It does not show incomplete subspace-level alignment, so it does not bear on V7.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Figure 2 and accompanying discussion; Sections 4.1 and 4.3 for training conditions.

rows.subject: ResNet20×8 models A and B (two independently initialized models)
rows.operation_detail: Compared top correlation values with top coefficients in the CCA Merge transformation.
rows.measure: Wasserstein distance between correlation and transformation-coefficient distributions, relative to the corresponding permutation comparison.
rows.value: Ratios are 0.15 and 0.04 for top 1, and 0.35 and 0.23 for top 2, across the two considered layers; layer-to-value assignments are not stated in the text.
rows.note: The authors say CCA coefficients visually resemble the correlation distributions more closely than permutation coefficients; this is a measure of correspondence between coefficients and correlations, not a direct score of full representational interchangeability.
rows.check: Diagnostic of how well CCA Merge coefficients fit the correlation distribution, normalized against permutation. This is the study's own method compared with another, not a measure of convergence or mapping loss.

rows.subject: VGG11
rows.operation_detail: Aligned two models with CCA Merge, averaged their parameters, and evaluated test accuracy.
rows.note: CCA Merge accuracy is below the average accuracy of the individual models.
rows.check: Merged accuracy after alignment plus parameter averaging. The accuracy loss reflects the averaging barrier, not loss from mapping one representation onto another, so it does not measure V4 or V7.

relationships.condition: Independently initialized ResNet20×8 models on CIFAR100, two merging layers
relationships.reason: Each neuron has several relatively high cross-model correlations, none near 1. The features are shared but distributed across units rather than matched one-to-one (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Each neuron correlated relatively highly with several neurons across models, but no correlation approached 1, indicating distributed correspondence.
